Biological Rationale: The CNS is protected by three meningeal membranes, cushioned by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), organized into gray matter (unmyelinated cell bodies/fibers) and white matter (myelinated axons), and develops from the embryonic dorsal neural tube. Incorrect Options: (1) White matter contains myelinated axons, and CSF is produced by choroid plexuses in brain ventricles, not white matter cell bodies. (2) The somatic and autonomic nervous systems are divisions of the peripheral nervous system (PNS), not the central nervous system (CNS).

title: Sense Organs
q: In the human retina, what is the correct sequence of cells through which visual signals are integrated before nerve impulses are sent to the brain?
opts: Ganglion cells synapse with bipolar cells, which in turn synapse with photoreceptor cells (rods and cones).
Bipolar cells synapse with ganglion cells, which in turn synapse with photoreceptor cells (rods and cones).
Photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) synapse with bipolar cells, which in turn synapse with ganglion cells.
Photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) synapse with ganglion cells, which in turn synapse with bipolar cells.
explanation: Correct Answer: Photoreceptor cells (rods and cones) synapse with bipolar cells, which in turn synapse with ganglion cells. Biological Rationale: In the retina, light stimulates photoreceptors (rods and cones) at the back layer. The electrical signal then travels forward: photoreceptors synapse with bipolar cells, which in turn synapse with ganglion cells. The axons of ganglion cells form the optic nerve to transmit impulses to the brain. Incorrect Options: (1), (2), and (4) show incorrect synaptic sequences of retinal cells.

title: Sense Organs
q: Why do cone cells provide a much sharper and more detailed image of an object compared to rod cells in the human retina?
opts: Fewer cone cells synapse on a single ganglion cell than rod cells, resulting in less convergence of visual signals.
Cone cells contain rhodopsin which absorbs all wavelengths of light, whereas rod cells only absorb blue light.
Ganglion cells directly synapse onto the cornea, bypassing the lens entirely when processing signals from cones.
Cones are larger and contain more nuclei per cell, allowing them to conduct impulses at a higher velocity.
explanation: Correct Answer: Fewer cone cells synapse on a single ganglion cell than rod cells, resulting in less convergence of visual signals. Biological Rationale: Cone cells provide high visual acuity (sharpness). In the fovea centralis, where cones are concentrated, there is a one-to-one relationship where a single cone synapses with a single bipolar cell, which connects to a single ganglion cell. This lack of convergence preserves the detail of the signal. In contrast, many rod cells converge onto a single ganglion cell, which increases light sensitivity but reduces sharpness. Incorrect Options: (1) Rhodopsin is the light-absorbing pigment in rods, not cones (which contain photopsins). (2) Ganglion cell axons form the optic nerve and synapse in the brain, not on the cornea or lens. (3) Cones are not multinucleated and do not have higher velocity propagation based on size.

title: Sense Organs
q: During visual accommodation in the human eye, what is the state of the ciliary muscle when focusing on a distant object versus a near object?
opts: The ciliary muscle is contracted when focusing on a distant object, and relaxed when focusing on a near object.
The ciliary muscle is relaxed when focusing on a distant object, and contracted when focusing on a near object.
The ciliary muscle is contracted for both distant and near objects, but relaxed only when the eye is closed.
The ciliary muscle is relaxed for both distant and near objects, as accommodation is controlled by the pupil size.
explanation: Correct Answer: The ciliary muscle is relaxed when focusing on a distant object, and contracted when focusing on a near object. Biological Rationale: Visual accommodation involves changing lens shape: to focus on distant objects, the ciliary muscle relaxes, increasing tension on suspensory ligaments and flattening the lens. To focus on near objects, the ciliary muscle contracts, releasing tension on suspensory ligaments, allowing the elastic lens to round up (become more convex) to bend light rays more. Incorrect Options: (1) describes the opposite muscle states. (2) and (3) are incorrect because the muscle state changes to focus near vs. far, and is not regulated by pupil size.

title: Sense Organs
q: In the human middle ear, how is the vibration pressure transferred and amplified from the tympanic membrane to the cochlea?
opts: Vibration is transferred from the stapes to the incus, and then to the malleus, which strikes the round window.
Vibration is transferred from the tympanic membrane directly to the auditory tube, bypassing the ossicles.
Vibration is transferred from the malleus to the incus, and then to the stapes, which strikes the oval window.
Vibration is transferred from the malleus directly to the cochlea via the vestibular nerve.
explanation: Correct Answer: Vibration is transferred from the malleus to the incus, and then to the stapes, which strikes the oval window. Biological Rationale: Sound waves vibrate the tympanic membrane (eardrum), which moves the three middle ear ossicles: first the malleus (hammer), then the incus (anvil), and finally the stapes (stirrup). The stapes vibrates against the oval window of the cochlea, transferring and amplifying the pressure waves into the fluid of the inner ear. Incorrect Options: (1) The ossicle sequence is incorrect, and the stapes strikes the oval window, not the round window (which serves to release fluid pressure). (2) The auditory tube equalizes air pressure but does not transmit sound vibrations to the cochlea. (3) Vibrations pass through the ossicles, not directly to the vestibular nerve.

title: Sense Organs
q: Which structures of the human inner ear are responsible for maintaining rotational equilibrium and gravitational equilibrium, respectively?
opts: Semicircular canals for rotational equilibrium, and the utricle and saccule for gravitational equilibrium.
The cochlea for rotational equilibrium, and the semicircular canals for gravitational equilibrium.
The vestibule for rotational equilibrium, and the organ of Corti for gravitational equilibrium.
The tympanic membrane for rotational equilibrium, and the ossicles for gravitational equilibrium.
explanation: Correct Answer: Semicircular canals for rotational equilibrium, and the utricle and saccule for gravitational equilibrium. Biological Rationale: Rotational (dynamic) equilibrium is detected by mechanoreceptors (hair cells in the crista ampullaris) in the semicircular canals. Gravitational (static) equilibrium, which detects head position relative to gravity and linear acceleration, is detected by hair cells in the maculae of the utricle and saccule (within the vestibule). Incorrect Options: (1) The cochlea is the organ of hearing, not equilibrium. (2) The organ of Corti (in the cochlea) is for hearing. (3) Tympanic membrane and ossicles are middle ear structures that transmit sound, not inner ear equilibrium receptors.

title: Sense Organs
q: Which somatic receptors are involved in reflex actions that maintain muscle tone?
opts: Nociceptors (such as free nerve endings)
Proprioceptors (such as muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs)
Cutaneous receptors (such as Pacinian corpuscles)
Chemoreceptors (such as olfactory cells)
explanation: Correct Answer: Proprioceptors (such as muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs) Biological Rationale: Proprioceptors are mechanoreceptors that send signals to the CNS regarding muscle stretch and joint position, helping maintain muscle tone and posture. They include muscle spindles (detecting muscle length changes) and Golgi tendon organs (detecting tendon tension). Incorrect Options: (1) Nociceptors are pain receptors. (2) Cutaneous receptors are sensory receptors in the skin for touch/temperature. (3) Chemoreceptors detect chemical concentrations (like taste/smell).

title: Sense Organs
q: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the layers and structures of the human eye?
correct: The sclera is the opaque outer layer, which becomes the transparent cornea in the front.
The choroid is the middle layer that contains blood vessels and forms the iris in the front.
The retina is the inner layer containing photoreceptors (rods and cones) and the fovea centralis.
opts: The sclera is the opaque outer layer, which becomes the transparent cornea in the front.
The fovea centralis is the region of the retina where the optic nerve connects, creating a blind spot.
The choroid is the middle layer that contains blood vessels and forms the iris in the front.
Rhodopsin is the light-absorbing pigment in cones, while cones also contain red, green, and blue opsin.
The retina is the inner layer containing photoreceptors (rods and cones) and the fovea centralis.
explanation:
Correct Answers: 
- The sclera is the opaque outer layer, which becomes the transparent cornea in the front.
- The choroid is the middle layer that contains blood vessels and forms the iris in the front.
- The retina is the inner layer containing photoreceptors (rods and cones) and the fovea centralis. Biological Rationale: The eye has three layers: the outer sclera (opaque white, becomes transparent cornea in front), the middle choroid (vascular, becomes iris and ciliary body in front), and the inner retina (sensory layer with rods, cones, and the fovea centralis). Incorrect Options: (1) The optic disc (not fovea centralis) is the blind spot where the optic nerve exits. (2) Rhodopsin is the pigment in rods, not cones.

opts: Meissner corpuscles

Merkel disks
